recent_posts.title: Embrace the monolith: Adding a new product to Aha!
recent_posts.summary: The post explores the options of starting a new product, either from a brand new codebase, microservices, or continuing with the existing monolithic codebase. It highlights the benefits of embracing the monolith and reusing existing code, as well as the challenges of implementing features and integrating with the billing system.

recent_posts.title: Blue Ridge Ruby: A Couple of Reflections
recent_posts.summary: Reflections from the Blue Ridge Ruby conference covering two main themes: the irreplaceable value of in-person developer gatherings and the current state of AI-assisted development for experienced Ruby/Rails developers. The author argues that small regional Ruby conferences foster genuine community in ways that don't scale to larger events. On AI, the key insight is that experienced developers who bring clear specifications and strong opinions about their stack can use tools like Claude or Codex to build at unprecedented speed, with output quality driven more by input clarity than model capability. A conference attendee's story of building a full companion app for the event is cited as a real-world example.

recent_posts.title: Avoid html_safe with Tag Helpers, safe_join, and sanitize
recent_posts.summary: Using html_safe in Rails bypasses XSS protection and is risky when user input is involved. Rails provides three safer alternatives: the tag helper for building HTML elements (auto-escapes content and attributes), safe_join for combining safe HTML fragments with potentially unsafe text, and sanitize for accepting user-provided HTML while stripping dangerous tags like script elements and event handlers. html_safe has legitimate uses only when content is fully controlled, such as output from trusted gems or truly static strings with no user input.

recent_posts.title: The Execution Boundary in Rails
recent_posts.summary: When Rails work leaves the request-response cycle via background jobs, after_commit callbacks, or async mailers, it crosses an execution boundary that fundamentally changes how the code behaves. Five key dimensions shift: time (state may change before the job runs), state (jobs re-enter from persisted data, not in-memory context), database visibility (jobs enqueued inside transactions may not see uncommitted records), failure model (retries make idempotency a correctness requirement, not a polish), and discoverability (lifecycle hooks hide side effects from the initiating code). Practical guidance includes revalidating state inside jobs, using after_commit deliberately, designing jobs as resumable idempotent operations, preferring explicit orchestration for multi-step business flows, and treating every boundary crossing as a design decision rather than a convenience.

recent_posts.title: Ten Years of Frontend
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough of modern Rails frontend development using Hotwire, Stimulus, and Turbo. The episode demonstrates building two Stimulus controllers — a hotkey controller that focuses a search field when '/' is pressed, and a filter controller with debounced form submission and a clear button — wired together in an ERB view with Turbo Frames for live search filtering.

recent_posts.title: A Vanilla Routing Experiment
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on experiment building client-side routing from scratch using only vanilla JavaScript and native browser APIs, without any SPA framework. Starting from a naive Router class, the author iteratively solves six real problems: view-specific logic bleeding into the router (solved with a view-based architecture and ES6 dynamic imports), duplicate browser history entries (solved by distinguishing user vs. browser navigation), broken deep links on static hosts (solved with a 404.html sessionStorage redirect trick), invalid route handling (custom 404 view), GitHub Pages subdirectory deployment (solved using import.meta.url to derive basePath at runtime), and regression testing (solved by adding Playwright BDD end-to-end tests). The conclusion is that vanilla routing is viable for very small projects or learning purposes, but the missing features (URL params, nested routes, route guards) and maintenance burden make frameworks the better choice for anything more complex.

recent_posts.title: Tiered API Rate Limits in Rails 8.2 with Dynamic rate_limit
recent_posts.summary: Rails 8.2 introduces dynamic options for the `rate_limit` controller macro, allowing `to:` and `within:` to accept procs or method names instead of only static values. This enables per-plan tiered rate limiting (free/pro/enterprise) directly in controllers without Rack::Attack or custom middleware. The post covers four practical patterns: tiered plan limits, burst plus sustained limits, anonymous vs authenticated users, and custom 429 JSON responses with Retry-After headers and instrumentation. Key caveats include cache store requirements for multi-server deployments, fixed-window behavior, and plan upgrade timing edge cases.

recent_posts.title: Ruby Classes
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to Ruby classes covering three categories: basic, whole value, and functional. Explores how each category maps to OOP principles like composition, inheritance, encapsulation, modularity, and reusability. Contrasts basic presenter classes with functional command-pattern classes, showing how dependency injection, the Forwardable module, and the #call method enable cleaner, more testable designs. Includes RSpec testing examples and references to gems like Initable for reducing boilerplate.

recent_posts.title: NPM: putting the brown in brownout
recent_posts.summary: NPM silently deprecated the legacy security audit endpoints used by Yarn v1 (`/-/npm/v1/security/audits`), causing `yarn audit` to return 410 errors with no public announcement. After contacting NPM support, the author learned this is a 'scheduled brownout' with full retirement on July 15, 2026, yet no changelog entry or public notice exists. The post criticizes GitHub/NPM for failing to communicate this breaking change to the ecosystem, leaving teams scrambling. The recommended migration path is to switch to the Bulk Advisory API or move to `npm audit` directly.

recent_posts.title: Welcome to Hanakai
recent_posts.summary: Hanakai is a new unified organization bringing together three major Ruby projects — Hanami, Dry, and Rom — under one shared community and brand. The announcement introduces a new website at hanakai.org, a refreshed visual identity, and a consolidated team. Upcoming plans include a new Dry Operation release, a feature-packed Hanami release candidate, new guides for Rails developers migrating to Hanami, and a 2026 sponsorship drive.

top_posts.title: Why chasing every new AI tool is a distraction from building
top_posts.summary: The rapid pace of AI tool releases creates pressure to constantly update workflows, but chasing every new model or tool is counterproductive. Finding a workflow that works and sticking with it allows developers to focus on building rather than perpetually optimizing. Being 80% optimal with a stable workflow is better than constantly pursuing 100% perfection, as the truly valuable tools will prove themselves over time while trends fade.

top_posts.title: Vibe Learning is Underrated
top_posts.summary: AI can facilitate skill acquisition through practical, just-in-time learning. The author shares how they overcame their challenges with bookkeeping by using QuickBooks alongside ChatGPT, which provided personalized guidance and explanations. This approach transformed a daunting task into a manageable one, demonstrating the potential of AI as a patient mentor that enables users to learn at their own pace and focus on practical application.

top_posts.title: Analyzing developer perspectives on test driven development adoption
top_posts.summary: A developer explores a Reddit discussion about Test-Driven Development adoption, analyzing various perspectives on TDD implementation. The post examines common misconceptions about TDD, discusses the differences between frontend and backend testing approaches, and critiques AI-generated tests. Key insights include focusing on test failure cases, treating code as a liability, and understanding that TDD doesn't require knowing the implementation beforehand. The author emphasizes that effective testing should provide value and support code changes, while acknowledging that TDD isn't always the right approach for every situation.

top_posts.title: Tailwind has won
top_posts.summary: Tailwind has emerged as the preferred CSS framework due to its extensive styles, excellent documentation, and flexibility. It is used in combination with a custom design system, allowing for easy style sharing across components.

top_posts.title: How to Choose a Node.js Framework
top_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide comparing popular Node.js frameworks including Express, Fastify, Koa, NestJS, and Next.js. Covers each framework's strengths, performance characteristics, learning curves, and ideal use cases. Express offers flexibility and ease of use, Fastify prioritizes performance, Koa provides modern minimalism, NestJS delivers enterprise-grade structure, and Next.js enables full-stack React development. Includes practical decision-making criteria based on project requirements like performance needs, team size, and application complexity.
